title: A scientific benchmark for elasto-plastic constitutive modeling - Part I: micro- and macroscopic experimental data set and benchmark problem
abstract: Abstract An accurate and diverse set of experimental data is essential for characterizing material behavior across different length scales and for calibrating the respective constitutive models. An independent validation experiment, the MUC-Test, is presented to validate such constitutive models. The benchmark dataset provides raw experimental data that serves as the basis for calibrating constitutive models of varying complexity. The material investigated is a dual-phase steel (DP800HHE). The conducted microscale experiments investigate the material properties at the grain level. These experiments include nanoindentation, electron backscatter diffraction, and in-situ synchrotron measurements to capture the material’s microstructural behavior. These data serve as the basis for generating representative volume elements and for phase-specific calibration of the crystal plasticity models. On the macroscale, a wide range of experiments has been conducted, including tensile, tension-compression, plane-strain, shear, layer-compression, and cyclic tensile tests. This data can be used to calibrate flow curves and yield locus curves. Part I of this benchmark paper series details the experiments and provides data for calibrating both microscopic and macroscopic models. It also introduces the benchmark problem based on the MUC-Test for validation of these models. Dataset https://zenodo.org/records/18431261

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Benchmarks are an essential part of the scientific process. They enable objective comparisons and independent evaluations of different methods within a field of study. One of the best-known benchmarks today is the “ImageNet” benchmark dataset [ 1 ], which contains more than 14 million labeled images. Since 2010, this benchmark and the annual competitions have made it possible to track the ongoing development of image recognition. The same applies to more engineering-oriented benchmarks, such as the “DIC Challenges” conducted under the auspices of the Society for Experimental Mechanics and iDICs [ 2 ].

In sheet metal forming research, different benchmark tasks are used to compare numerical simulations against measurements of deep drawn parts or simpler experiments. In the benchmark study by Allen et al. [ 3 ], parameters were provided to calibrate flow curves and yield locus functions to simulate the forming process of an aluminum pillar. The participants’ numerical predictions were evaluated at three cross-sections after springback using a geometric comparison. The ESAFORM 2024 benchmark [ 4 ] focuses on the geometric accuracy of a part produced by single point incremental forming. In this study, multiple research institutes contributed experimental results to systematically investigate the influence of process strategies and tool paths on the final part geometry.

Also widely known are the S-rail benchmark [ 5 ] and the U-bending benchmark [ 6 ], introduced at NUMISHEET conferences to validate advances in springback prediction. These benchmarks are still often used to validate new constitutive models [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ], compare finite-element solver approaches [ 10 ,  11 ], or conduct parameter studies [ 12 ]. Yet, all of these benchmarks were designed to validate macroscopic forming simulations and do not provide multiscale, batch-consistent calibration data.

Ongoing advances in constitutive modeling are continuously increasing the experimental effort required for model calibration. The phenomenological Yld2004-18p yield criterion, e.g., requires nine independent experiments for calibration [ 13 ]. When combining this with a kinematic hardening model, the data space expands further. This is where current benchmark datasets reach their limits. One promising approach is to calibrate such complex material models using a virtual laboratory [ 14 ]. The study of Liu et al. [ 15 ] demonstrates that constitutive models calibrated via crystal plasticity simulation (CPFEM) tests accurately predict springback and deformation behaviors. They also used the U-bending benchmark for validation.

Coppieters et al. [ 16 ] also use the virtual laboratory approach to calibrate a Yld2000-2d model. Here, a representative volume element (RVE) of a single-phase ferritic steel was calibrated using a tensile test in the rolling direction (RD) and an orientation distribution function. Nine load paths in the first quadrant of the stress space were generated to calibrate the Yld2000-2d and compared with the corresponding experiments. These investigations enabled the creation of experimental and virtually calibrated yield locus curves. Both approaches were validated using the bulge test. Coppieters et al. obtained equally good simulation results for the bulge test using both approaches.

The process becomes more complex when calibrating an RVE with individual models for ferrite and martensite for a dual-phase (DP) steel. A tensile test is insufficient here because it does not provide a unique solution. Jeon et al. [ 17 ] demonstrate that their elasto-visco-plastic self-consistent crystal plasticity model can be used to determine the lattice strains from a tensile-compression test on a DP1000. Using a dataset containing lattice strains for ferrite and martensite, it is possible to perform phase-specific optimization of the elastic and plastic material parameters. For validation, Jeon et al. also use the U-bending experiment. However, a problem here is that the U-bending experiment was not performed on the same DP1000 batch as the tensile-compression test and other tests they use for calibration. These studies demonstrate that benchmark datasets intended for long-term use should provide data for generating RVEs and calibrating phase-specific constitutive models.

Despite these developments in virtual calibration approaches, current benchmark datasets still lack comprehensive multiscale experimental data. As a result, they are only partially suitable for the calibration and validation of modern constitutive models, particularly when phase-specific behavior needs to be captured. The aim of this study is therefore to provide a batch-consistent benchmark dataset for DP800HHE (high-hole expansion) steel, enabling calibration and validation across multiple scales. The dataset is designed to support both macroscopic finite element models and microstructure-based approaches. A brief introduction to macroscopic and microscopic constitutive modeling approaches for plasticity is provided in Appendix  A . Part II of the benchmark paper series provides examples of how to use the provided experimental dataset to calibrate microscopic and macroscopic material models [ 18 ].

In addition, the validation experiment MUC-Test proposed by Eder et al. [ 19 ] is introduced in this paper. This experiment minimizes the influence of friction effects. Part II of the benchmark paper series evaluates the benchmark results submitted by participants in the NUMISHEET 2025 Scientific Benchmark and presents the underlying experimental ground truth for the MUC-Test validation experiment [ 18 ].

sections.heading: Macroscopic experiments
paragraphs: This section describes the macroscopic test methods used. Tensile and compressive tests were performed to assess deformation and failure behavior. The tests included monotonic tensile, cyclic tensile, tensile-compressive, plane strain, shear, and layer compression. These tests were conducted on an AllRound Line Z 150 universal testing machine from ZwickRoell GmbH & Co. KG, equipped with a LaserXtens non-contact strain gauge. To capture digital image correlation (DIC) data, the Aramis SRX from Carl Zeiss GOM Metrology GmbH was used. In addition, Nakajima and bulge tests were performed on a BUP1000 sheet metal forming machine from ZwickRoell GmbH & Co. KG. This machine was equipped with the Aramis 4M DIC system from Carl Zeiss GOM Metrology GmbH. Both DIC systems operate in accordance with the VDI 2626 [ 20 ] and VDI 2634-1 [ 21 ] directives for optical measurement devices.

sections.heading: Tensile tests - uniaxial load
paragraphs: The tensile test, defined in ISO 6892-1 [ 22 ], is a standardized method for determining mechanical properties of materials under tensile load at room temperature. The test starts by preparing a specimen. To prevent changes in the martensite and ferrite phases, the samples for this and subsequent experiments were prepared using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Tensile specimens were produced according to DIN 50125 [ 23 ], shape H standards. The specimens had a parallel length of 75 mm, a gauge length of 50 mm, and a width of 12.5 mm. The tested DP800HHE had a thickness of 1.49 mm and was uncoated. The thickness and width of all samples were measured at three points using a micrometer. The specimen was then clamped in a tensile testing machine that applied controlled forces while measuring its length. A preload of 50 N was applied. This results in a pre-stress of 2.68 MPa, which is well below the onset for yielding and below the maximum recommended by ISO 6892-1.

During the test, the specimen is continuously deformed as the applied force increases. Changes in the applied force and specimen elongation are recorded. Both a laser extensometer and a DIC system were used to measure length changes. The test typically determines parameters such as yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation at break. These parameters were measured in a test with a constant traverse speed of 0.15 mm/s. This gives an elongation rate of about 0.002 1/s. Surface temperature changes were measured with a PT1000 sensor attached to the specimen. This made it possible to determine the onset of yielding by temperature, as described in [ 24 ,  25 – 26 ].

sections.heading: Tensile tests - cyclic load
Tension-compression test
paragraphs: The tension-compression test is a setup used to characterize the mechanical response of materials to load reversal. To enhance the stability of the testing setup during compression, an anti-buckling support mechanism is integrated. The support was designed in accordance with the anti-buckling device proposed in [ 28 ]. Four screws with metric thread M4 on each side provide axial support for the sample. These screws were tightened to 3 Nm of torque prior to the commencement of the test. It has a measuring window for setting the extensometer’s initial length to 12 mm. The strains are captured using a non-contact extensometer. All experiments were subjected to a preload of 50 N. Throughout the testing process, the elongation levels were incrementally increased by 1% of the engineering strain for each additional sample examined. After tensile loads, the sample is compressed to its initial length and, in the third step, relieved of external forces.

Figure  3  illustrates the seven experiments conducted in a true stress-strain diagram, each with an engineering strain of 2% to 8%. Tensile, compressive, and force relief procedures were conducted at a constant crosshead speed of 0.15 mm/s. All experiments were carried out in RD. The data obtained from the experimental procedure can be utilized for calibrating a kinematic hardening model, such as the Chaboche-Rousselier model [ 29 ] or the Yoshida-Uemori model [ 27 ], which is particularly relevant in accurately predicting springback in sheet metal forming. For example, this model is applicable when material passes through a drawbead and experiences both tensile and compressive stresses. Notably, the kinematic hardening effect demonstrated in this experiment was first identified by Bauschinger [ 30 ]. Fig. 3 True stress-strain diagram of seven DP800HHE tension-compression tests to investigate the kinematic hardening in between 2% and 8% engineering strain, individual cycles were controlled by engineering strain and increased by 1% per experiment

Layer compression test
paragraphs: In the layer compression test, round specimens with a diameter of 15 mm were cut from the DP800HHE material using a laser. 2  The stack consisted of eleven DP800HHE specimens compressed between two parallel plates. The middle three specimens were selected for evaluation because they exhibit uniform load distribution and experience the least friction. To minimize interaction with the pressure plates, the stack was decoupled using a lanolin-based lubricant and a Teflon sheet. Prior to the start of the experiment, the lengths of the three specimens in RD and transverse directions, as well as their thickness, were measured using a micrometer. After the compressive force was applied, the resulting deformation was quantified. This experimental setup was proposed by Vegter and An [ 34 ] and by Merklein and Kuppert [ 35 ].

With these measurements, the biaxial r-value can be calculated. Table  1  presents mean measurement results for each layer from three tests, where measurements were taken after a 180 kN load. In another test series, a 200 kN load was used. In both series, the crosshead had a constant velocity of 0.01 mm/s. Force signals shown in Fig.  7  are measured with a piezoelectric sensor, while displacement was recorded based on crosshead movement. sections.heading: Nakajima experiment
paragraphs: In the Nakajima experiment, according to ISO 12004 [ 36 ], the material is deformed until it necks or fractures, enabling investigation of its forming limit curve (FLC) and safe deformation boundaries. The test setup and specimen geometries follow the ISO 12004 standard. The punch speed was 1 mm/s. The clamping force between the blankholder and the die with a locking bead was 600 kN. Lanolin is used to lubricate the punch and reduce friction. A soft polyvinyl chloride sheet is placed between the punch and the sheet. Another layer of lanolin is applied between the polyvinyl chloride and the specimen. A piezoelectric sensor recorded the forces required for the experiment. Surface deformations were measured by a DIC system operating at 10 Hz. These data were used to calculate the major and minor strains. The line method and the time-dependent evaluation method [ 37 ] were used for the analysis and are available in the dataset.

Specimens with parallel sample lengths of 30 mm, 50 mm, 70 mm, 90 mm, 110 mm, 125 mm, and a full sample (235 mm) were used to investigate the FLC points. To ensure the reliability of the results, each test was conducted three times, and the data were analyzed statistically. Figure  8  illustrates the force-displacement curve of one specimen of each conducted geometry until failure, along with the FLC conducted in this manner. Fig. 8 a ) Force-displacement curves of seven Nakajima experiments of the respective specimen geometry for each FLC point;  b ) resulting FLC, determined using the line method with nine lines for each support point

sections.heading: Microscopic experiments
paragraphs: This section describes microscopic experiments, including optical emission spectrometry (OES), nanoindentation, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and in-situ synchrotron measurements. These methods enable the properties of DP800HHE steel to be investigated at the microstructural level. Grain size effects and phase distribution are analyzed with regard to mechanical properties. The experiments investigate the relationship between microstructure and macroscopic behavior. This characterization can be used to create an RVE, calibrate CPFEM constitutive models, or validate CPFEM constitutive models calibrated by inverse optimization from macroscopic experiments.

sections.heading: Optical emission spectrometer
paragraphs: The OES method analyzes chemical composition by detecting spectra produced when matter interacts with electromagnetic radiation. In this approach, spectral lines from specific atomic energy levels are analyzed. A DP800HHE specimen was tested at six surface points to assess homogeneity and determine its elemental composition. The OES results and corresponding standard deviations are presented in Table  2 . sections.heading: Scanning electron microscope and electron backscatter diffraction
paragraphs: In this study, SEM and EBSD were employed to scan and characterize the microstructural components of the DP800HHE steel. The SEM images provided offer a detailed view of the microstructural phases by SE2 and InLens detectors, as shown in Fig.  9 . This SE2 detector (Fig.  9 , left) is situated at a distance from the sample and can capture secondary electrons emitted from a broader area. It is suitable for observing the overall surface morphology and larger features of the sample. The InLens detector (Fig.  9 , right) is positioned closer to the electron beam axis, to capture secondary electrons emitted from a very small area near the beam interaction point. It is ideal for examining fine structures and smaller features. From the SEM images, it can be deduced that the DP800HHE steel predominantly comprises martensite and ferrite, which contribute to its high strength and moderate ductility. The possible presence of bainite and retained austenite, though minimal, can influence the overall mechanical properties, such as toughness and hardness. Fig. 9 SEM images of the DP800HHE showing various microstructural phases. Left: SE2 detector image highlighting the overall surface morphology. Right: InLens detector image providing detailed surface features. Key phases identified include Martensite (M), Ferrite (F), Bainite (B), and Retained Austenite (RA)

Deformation of the DP800HHE increases the average misorientation within the grains; the combination of these visualizations (Fig.  11 ) demonstrates the effect of deformation on the material’s microstructure [ 40 ]. The histogram quantifies changes in the misorientation distribution, while the microstructure maps visually illustrate them. 11% of pre-strained samples have higher KAM values than the raw DP800HHE, indicating increased internal strain and potential defects. This is evidenced by the shift in the histogram and the more prominent warm-colored areas in the right microstructure map compared to the left. sections.heading: Nanoindentation
In-situ synchrotron measurement
paragraphs: As described in “ Tensile tests - uniaxial load ” section, the sample was produced following DIN 50125 shape H standards with a parallel length of 75 mm, a gauge length of 50 mm, and a width of 12.5 mm. The thickness was about 1.49 mm. The sample was cut out of the sheet parallel to the RD. During the measurement, an uniaxial tensile test, as described in “ Tensile tests - uniaxial load ” section, was conducted at an elongation rate of approximately 0.0004 1/s. The elongation rate was chosen to obtain a sufficient number of measurement points in the elastoplastic region.

sections.heading: Texture measurement
paragraphs: Measuring the crystallographic texture is necessary to identify possible preferential orientations that could lead to anisotropic material behavior. To measure the texture, the sample is rotated successively, and diffractograms are collected in transmission geometry at each rotation step. The preferred crystalline orientation can be deduced from the intensity variations of the diffracted Debye-Scherrer rings.

sections.heading: Validation experiment
paragraphs: The provided experimental benchmark data can be utilized to calibrate constitutive models for forming simulations. To assess the quality of this constitutive model for representing the material at hand, an independent validation experiment is necessary. The MUC-Test, proposed in [ 19 ,  48 ], is to be employed in the benchmark for this purpose.

sections.heading: Experimental setup
Friction reduction of the validation experiment
Comparison parameters for validation
paragraphs: In the benchmark task, participants are required to set up a digital twin using the provided geometry and to run a simulation of the experiment using their calibrated constitutive models for the DP800HHE. In contrast to the approach proposed in [ 19 ], the full deformation field should not be used for comparison purposes. Instead, for validation, only major and minor strains along the xz- and yz-planes passing through the origin at the top of the sheet material, as shown in orange in Fig.  17 , should be considered. Figure  18  shows the DIC measurement results for a DP600, in which the RD was located along the x-direction, as an example of the strain distribution in the two evaluation sections. The representative strains shown were recorded at a punch stroke of 25 mm for the 70 mm specimen and both 16 mm for the 110 mm and 230 mm specimens. These strains are dependent on the punch stroke and sample geometry, and should be evaluated for the benchmark task at the punch stroke of Table  4 , where a displacement of 0.00 mm is the initial contact of the punch with the specimen. Figure  18 a shows that the three different specimen widths span a wide range in the minor strain region. For this reason, the MUC-Test is particularly well-suited as a validation experiment for material models in sheet metal forming.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook
paragraphs: This work introduces a batch-consistent experimental dataset for calibrating elasto-plastic constitutive models using DP800HHE steel. The micro- and macroscale investigations enable consistent use of models across different length scales, ranging from typical phenomenological models commonly used in FEM sheet metal forming analyses to phase-specific CPFEM models using RVEs. Microscale methods such as nanoindentation, EBSD, and in-situ synchrotron diffraction provide phase- and grain-specific data on deformation mechanisms. Macroscale experiments capture anisotropy, hardening, and complex loading conditions. Unlike existing benchmarks, this dataset achieves full batch consistency for both micro- and macroscale experiments. The benchmark problem first requires selecting an appropriate set of experiments to calibrate a chosen constitutive model. Next, it involves simulating the MUC-Test validation experiments to evaluate and compare the calibrated models. Part II of the benchmark paper series provides a detailed analysis and assessment of submitted models using the experimental MUC-Test reference data, enabling an objective comparison of current modeling methods across different length scales, as a basis for further development in the elasto-plastic modeling of sheet metal materials [ 18 ].
